analysis.one_liner: Caps speculative trading in oil, gas, and farm commodities and closes foreign-exchange loopholes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2008 by Senator Levin with two cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: After oil prices hit record highs in 2008, this bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to set hard limits on how large a speculative bet any one trader could hold in energy and agricultural futures. It would have closed a gap that let U.S. traders place bets through overseas exchanges to dodge American limits, required large off-exchange swap deals and index funds to report their positions, made public monthly data separating speculators from real hedgers, and added 100 enforcement staff at the CFTC. It died in committee without a single hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses paying gasoline, diesel, heating oil, natural gas, and electricity bills, who bear the brunt of price spikes; also farmers and other genuine physical hedgers who need futures prices that reflect actual supply and demand rather than speculative flows.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC to issue rules setting position limits on energy and agricultural futures within fixed deadlines — a proposed rule within 90 days and a final rule within 180 days of enactment.

Bars foreign exchanges from giving U.S. traders direct access to their systems for energy contracts that settle against U.S. prices unless the foreign exchange publishes comparable daily trading data and enforces comparable position limits — closing the route around U.S. rules through overseas markets.

Gives the CFTC authority to require large over-the-counter swap transactions to be reported, and to force any U.S.-connected trader to reduce or liquidate positions on a foreign exchange to prevent manipulation or excessive speculation.

Requires the CFTC to publish monthly data breaking out index funds and passive long-only positions, and speculative positions versus bona fide physical hedgers, so the public can see who is driving prices.
Directs the CFTC to review whether index trading is distorting price discovery, and to add at least 100 full-time enforcement employees to energy futures markets.

Creates a cabinet-level Working Group on Energy Markets to investigate speculation's effect on energy prices and recommend further laws, and directs FERC to investigate the role of financial institutions in natural gas markets.

analysis.who_pays: Investment banks and hedge funds running large commodity and swap positions, index fund managers who package commodity bets for investors, and overseas exchanges that sell U.S. traders a way around American limits; all face hard position caps, new reporting, and possible forced position reductions.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose limits and a working-group apparatus before its own studies (on speculation's effect on prices and on the international regulatory regime) were complete, effectively regulating first and studying the evidence later.

The 'major market disturbance' power lets the CFTC order traders to liquidate positions whenever it finds a market disruption from manipulation, excessive speculation, or even government action — broad discretionary authority over private contracts, with the bill itself providing that overseas contracts remain enforceable so affected traders could not easily recover losses.

Economists disagreed over how much of the 2008 oil price spike came from speculation versus supply, demand, and the falling dollar; if fundamentals drove most of the price move, position limits would restrict hedging liquidity without lowering prices much for consumers.

Because the foreign-board rules reach only contracts that settle against U.S.-listed prices, pure offshore trading could migrate to markets entirely outside the bill's reach, unless the international working group succeeded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculative money materially inflated 2008 energy prices, the position limits, transparency requirements, and offshore loophole closure would directly protect every household's fuel bill at a cost confined to large traders — a favorable trade. The honest caveat is that the causes of the price spike were contested and the bill's own studies were designed to answer that question only after the limits took effect; it also granted the CFTC unusually broad power to order forced liquidations. On balance the bill targeted a real, documented regulatory gap — U.S. rules that stopped at the border of U.S. exchanges — but the evidence for how much consumers would have gained was not settled.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced in late September 2008 and sat there, without even a hearing, until the Congress ended in early January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Carl Levin introduced the bill on September 25, 2008, with Senators Jeff Bingaman and Tom Harkin as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large commodity traders, swap dealers, and index fund managers kept operating under the pre-2008 rules, with no hard position limits on energy futures and foreign exchanges still able to serve U.S. traders outside American limits. Consumers got no new protection from energy price swings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big commodity traders and swap dealers

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats sponsored the bill; no Republican is on record supporting or opposing it, and the committee never acted, so no recorded vote shows the partisan split.

industries.industry: Investment banks, hedge funds, and swap dealers with large energy and commodity positions
industries.note: The bill imposes hard position limits, mandatory reporting of large off-exchange swaps, and authority to force liquidations when the CFTC finds excessive speculation. These desks profit from unlimited speculative positions in markets whose price swings hit consumers at the pump and the meter.

industries.industry: Commodity index funds and their managers
industries.note: The bill requires detailed reporting from index traders and swap dealers, directs the CFTC to review whether index trading distorts price discovery, and publishes monthly data on passive long-only positions. Index funds profit when the underlying commodity prices rise, a cost borne by energy consumers.

industries.industry: Foreign exchanges offering U.S. traders direct access (the offshore loophole)
industries.note: The bill conditions direct access for U.S. traders on the foreign exchange imposing comparable position limits and publishing comparable daily trading data, closing the route around U.S. rules through foreign markets.

industries.industry: U.S. commodity futures exchanges and clearinghouses
industries.note: They face new oversight, position limits, and position-accountability enforcement on their contracts, plus higher compliance burdens. In exchange, trading that otherwise fled to foreign markets must meet U.S.-comparable standards, and genuine hedging liquidity is preserved by the bill's good-faith hedging provisions.

Producers keep the ability to hedge physical sales (the bill preserves bona fide hedging and existing agricultural limits), but face new company-specific reporting on inventories, storage, and purchase commitments to the Energy Information Administration. High speculation-driven prices had fattened producer revenues, which the bill's limits could temper.
